content: A nuchal cord occurs when the umbilical cord becomes wrapped around the fetal neck in a 360-degree loop. Classification A Type A nuchal cord refers to a situation where the cord is wrapped around the neck. A Type B nuchal cord involves a hitch configuration, where the cord is not wrapped around the neck. In cases of a Type B nuchal cord, a cesarean section delivery may be recommended, although it is not always necessary. Diagnosis Doppler ultrasound is an effective diagnostic tool for identifying the presence of a nuchal cord. It can also determine the orientation of the loop around the fetal neck. Prognosis and Treatment Nuchal cords can be managed through home fetal monitoring. While a nuchal cord can be a potential cause of stillbirth, it is a preventable condition. The umbilical cord should not be clamped or cut until it has stopped pulsating, which can take upwards of 20 minutes after birth. This is particularly important in cases of a nuchal cord, as the child continues to receive blood and oxygen to the brain through the cord. As a general rule, the umbilical cord should only be cut after it has ceased pulsating, ensuring that all the blood from the placenta has been transferred to the child.
